title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
summary: You get an unsorted list of integers `nums`. Pick values from it that form an unbroken chain, each exactly 1 more than the one before, like 4, 5, 6, 7; they can come from anywhere in the list. Return the length of the longest such chain, or 0 if `nums` is empty. A value that repeats counts once. The whole search has to run in O(n) time.

examples.explanation: 5, 6, 7 and 8 are all in the list. 30 and 31 form a shorter chain.
-1, 0, 1, 2 and 3 are all present. The second 3 does not make the chain longer.

approaches.twist: Put all the values in a set, and walk upward only from a value x whose x − 1 is missing, so each chain is walked once.
Sort the values, then scan once, growing the current chain while each value is one more than the last and skipping repeats.
approaches.note: Works with little extra space if you sort in place, but sorting takes O(n log n) time. The target is O(n).

approaches.twist: Put every value in a set, and from each value count upward while the next value is also in the set.
approaches.note: Works, but counting up from every value walks the same chain again and again, so one long chain makes it O(n²). The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: A chain's values are scattered through the list. Sorting would line them up, but it costs O(n log n), so look neighbors up in a set instead.

signals.phrase: exactly 1 more than the one before
signals.meaning: Each step of a chain is a lookup: is x + 1 in the set? And if x − 1 is in it too, x is not where a chain starts, so skip it.
Sorting is O(n log n), so it is out. Starting a walk only at the first value of a chain means each value is visited at most twice: O(n) in total.
Building a set drops the repeats before you start.

constraintReading: len(nums) can reach 10⁵, and the required O(n) time rules out sorting, which is O(n log n). Values reach ±10⁹, far too spread out for an array indexed by value, so use a set: O(1) lookups for O(n) space. Walking up only from the first value of each chain keeps the total work O(n).

related.relation: Also looks up a neighboring value in O(1) instead of scanning for it: x − 1 and x + 1 here, target − x there.
